---
title: "D2 Data"
---

## The generating process

All data come from one generator, `shared/data_generator.py`, run with the platform seed
from `shared/config.py`:

```python
SEED = 42
```

The generator works in the order a validator would want to reason about it:

1. **Observable features first** — firmographics, financial statements, bureau history and
   the loan request, each drawn from a stated distribution.
2. **A latent default logit** built from a subset of those features plus unobserved noise.
   The true probability of default and the default outcome itself are drawn from it.
3. **Downstream outcomes** — whether the loan was booked, the rate it was quoted, and, for
   booked loans, a monthly behavioural history, later deterioration and whether a line
   increase would have gone well.

It writes three files, committed so that every stage of the workshop is self-sufficient:

| File | One row per | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| `shared/data/raw/businesses.parquet` | applicant | {{< var score.n_applicants >}} |
| `shared/data/raw/portfolio.parquet` | booked account | {{< var score.n_booked >}} |
| `shared/data/raw/panel.parquet` | booked account and month | the booked accounts × `PANEL_MONTHS` |

`python verify.py` checks all three row counts on every run. The generator's design,
including which features drive default and which deliberately do not, is the subject of
the Session 1 reading note (`workshop/reading/S1-data-generation.pdf`) and of the
explanation pages on synthetic data and leakage ([Explain](../explain/index.qmd)).

## Data quality

Because the data are generated, the usual quality failures — missing values, bad joins,
stale extracts — are absent by construction. The Session 1 data-quality report
(`python -m shared.data_quality`, written to `reports/data_quality.md`) still records row
counts, target rates, a null audit and the distributions of key features, so that a
regenerated dataset can be compared with the committed one. A validator should read this
section as a statement about the method, not as assurance about real data (D1).

## Two populations: applicants and booked

Every applicant has an outcome, because the generator gives one to everyone. A real bank
only observes outcomes for the loans it books. The platform keeps both:

- **Applicants** — all {{< var score.n_applicants >}}. The scorecard and the adjudication
  model train and are gated on a split of this population.
- **Booked** — the {{< var score.n_booked >}} applicants the generator marks as booked.
  The booking decision is drawn from the true PD with noise: it stands in for the bank's
  historical lending decision, not for the adjudication model's output. Pricing, early
  warning and line increase operate on this population only.

The difference matters most for discrimination. A model can rank the whole applicant
population well because it separates obvious declines from obvious approvals, then rank
the booked population — the only one the bank lends to — much less well. D4 measures the
scorecard on both and reports the gap as an open finding.

## Leakage controls

A column leaks if it would not exist at the moment the decision is made. The platform keeps
one deny-list, in `shared/config.py`:

```python
LEAKAGE_COLUMNS = [
    "pd_default_origination",     # DGP ground-truth PD
    "default",                    # scorecard/adjudication target
    "risk_based_rate",            # priced from the true PD
    "booked",                     # funding decision (post-adjudication)
    "deterioration_next_6_12mo",  # downstream early-warning target
    "line_increase_good",         # downstream line-increase target
]
```

It is enforced in three places, so no single oversight lets a column through:

1. **At feature construction.** The adjudication, early-warning and line-increase feature
   builders (`*/src/feature_engineering.py`) raise an error if any denied column is in
   their feature list.
2. **At training.** The same three modules' `train.py` assert that their feature list and
   the deny-list are disjoint before fitting.
3. **In the test suite.** `tests/test_leakage.py` asserts that the scorecard's and the
   adjudication model's feature lists are disjoint from the deny-list, and that every denied
   column actually exists in the data — a deny-list of typos protects nothing.

The scorecard's feature list is a fixed list of {{< var score.n_features >}} named
columns, checked by the third control. Two further rules sit beside the deny-list:

- **Downstream modules consume the saved model's output, never the generator's truth.**
  Adjudication, early warning and line increase read the score and PD from
  `predict_score_pd`, the scorecard's own scoring function.
- **Some denied columns are still used, as facts about the book, never as inputs to a
  model.** Pricing reads `booked` to know which loans exist and `risk_based_rate` as the
  rate each one was quoted, so that it can flag the ones priced below the hurdle.

## Exclusions

No applicant is excluded from any sample. Train and test splits are stratified on the
outcome with the platform seed; each module chapter states its own split and population.
